title: It Builds. Can We Ship It?

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Hello. I'm Sam. I write C plus plus, I use Make, and I trust tools more after they've disappointed me in a predictable way.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: And I'm LitAI, your personification of Literate A I. I bring specifications, tests, and an unreasonable interest in what actually reaches the user.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: We're taking a small adventure from it builds on my machine to someone else can use it. There may be disagreements.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: There will definitely be evidence. We'll set up, build a new project, adopt an existing C plus plus library, and discuss life after the demo.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: For the record, I know what best practices are. I've read several postmortems in which we rediscovered them.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Exactly. This isn't remedial software engineering. It's making the practices you already value happen reliably, even when your new colleague types at industrial speed.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Ah, agents. Amazingly fast. Occasionally an artisanal producer of A I slop. Now available in enterprise quantities.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Speed multiplies whatever process surrounds it. Give an agent vague intent and no independent checks, and it can industrialize your misunderstanding.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: So agents need oversight. Unlike experienced engineers, who have evolved beyond checklists.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Yes. That explains why production incidents stopped happening when senior titles were invented.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Fine. We all need it. I'd prefer the oversight to be executable, rather than another document everyone agrees to ignore.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: That's the point. The harness gives your agent a structured route from intent to proof. It doesn't replace engineering judgment, or make every generated answer correct.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: First obstacle: where do I get it? Please don't begin with a machine you configured three months ago.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: The public repository is on screen. This film uses a development checkout; follow its installation documentation and choose a reviewed revision, not a mysterious package name.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And on this Mac, the starting kit?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Python three eleven or newer, Git, and Make. Clone the repository, enter it, then make install. These setup panels are a walkthrough, not a recording of installation.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Does make install install every compiler I've ever offended?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Read its prerequisite prompts and approve only the intended changes. It selects prerequisites for your platform. Windows has its own documented setup path.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Installation finished. My shell says command not found. A classic welcome ceremony.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Check the prefix the installer reported, then your PATH. Run litai dash dash version and litai doctor. A diagnostic is useful information, not an invitation to ignore it.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And installing the harness logs me into the coding agent?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Separate step. Authenticate your selected supported coding CLI. This session uses Codex with an explicit model selector. Credentials stay off camera, and model usage can cost money.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Good. Now let's do something real before our onboarding develops a sequel.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Here begins recorded execution, edited into a terminal replay. Waiting is compressed; results aren't invented. First, a read-only create plan for a disposable application.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: It tells me what it will create before touching the project. Python and Make for this first run. The language choice isn't the specification.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Right. Review the target and parent, then apply with acknowledgement. For automation, bind apply to the printed plan identity so a changed proposal cannot slip through.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Here's the inherited greeting-card contract: a name and messages go in; a greeting, normalized recipient identifier, message count and word count come out. Let's inspect that promise.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: The Component owns observable behavior. Flavors select language, build system and platform. Skills guide technique. We haven't outsourced the definition of correct to the agent.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Let's ask it to implement that promise. And explicitly allow it to compile and execute here. This is a disposable demo, not a production deployment.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Rebuild drives the lifecycle. Generation is only one stage: current tests, execution and independent acceptance still have to pass. The model selector is visible in the command.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Now we're looking at code the agent actually generated in this run. Not a hand-written example disguised as an agent success story.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Read it. Does recipient normalization match the contract? Does counting handle Unicode whitespace? Fluency isn't evidence. The implementation must survive those questions.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And these are the generated tests. Useful, but the author grading its own homework isn't our entire quality department.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Exactly. Native tests and independent acceptance have different jobs. Passing a self-written test suite doesn't automatically prove the written product contract.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And it failed. Missing messages. The specification requires messages, but this acceptance invocation supplied only a name. That's not the agent ignoring the contract.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Correct. We found an inheritance defect: the richer parent Component got the simple starter's verifier. Here are our independently calculated acceptance cases for the actual written contract.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Two messages, six words. The expected recipient follows the specified normalization. We changed the verifier to match intent, not to flatter the generated code.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: This is a demo-local correction, not a framework fix. The inheritance defect is tracked for repair. We rerun the complete lifecycle before claiming success.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: So this is a current result, with its actual passes and skips visible. Not a green screenshot borrowed from a different revision.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Keep the inputs and model selection consistent. A receipt is evidence about exact work, not a lifetime warranty on everything named hello.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Now packaging. The part of my old workflow described by a folder named release stuff.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: We build a local wheel from the accepted application. Packaging, package verification, publishing and releasing are distinct decisions. No registry upload happens in this film.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: A verified package is better than a confidently named zip. I remain emotionally attached to the zip.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: You may keep the attachment. For your next feature, change observable intent, review it, then regenerate and re-run the gates. Don't make generated source your hidden specification.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.chapter: Use the machines you already own
turns.text: Do I need to buy a fleet to get started? I already own several computers that contribute mainly fan noise.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Start here, locally. The session just used this machine. Existing compatible machines can be workers; you don't need a new hosted service merely to begin.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: So target means what I want to build, and worker means where it happens?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Yes. Keep worker addresses and credentials out of project authority. Use the synthetic worker and test examples, and let litai config paths locate your private configuration.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Then verify the selected model and probe the machine before I send it a long job. Start with one compatible cell, not the entire matrix.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Exactly. This section is a remote-worker walkthrough, not proof of an SSH run. Check the toolchain and separate agent login on each actual worker.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: The new project was deliberately tiny. What about code that already earns its keep? Preferably C plus plus, so I can recognize my own anxiety.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Let's use TinyXML2, a public XML library, at the recorded commit. This is our disposable demonstration, not an upstream adoption or an endorsement by its maintainers.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Read-only inspection first. It discovers the existing language and build tools. And there's a Git recovery point before any source moves.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Apply wraps the existing project and runs the authorized baseline and parity work. Watch the actual build evidence. We are not replacing the C plus plus implementation.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: There's the existing source in its retained implementation location. The library didn't disappear into a Markdown file.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Now run the retained harness. It rebuilds and tests the preserved implementation in disposable custody. The recorded result tells us what passed, not what we hoped.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: CMake, the actual C plus plus targets, and CTest. Familiar tools. The new thing is the explicit evidence around them.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: The rehearsal exposed another framework bug: a new CTest summary format wasn't counted. We fixed the parser, not the test result, and reran the real harness.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Then publish the finalized test receipt to this local project. Publish here doesn't mean upload TinyXML2 anywhere.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Correct. Now advance to retained. Original source remains release authority. A recorded baseline is valuable already, without pretending we completed a native rewrite.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And the later stages? I suspect there's a catch called actually understanding the software.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: A good catch. Draft specifications, review them, then qualify clean regeneration against independent behavior evidence. Move one boundary at a time. These later stages aren't demonstrated as complete here.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: So early adoption buys me repeatable evidence and clearer handoffs. Specification-led shipping comes later, when we've earned it. That sounds considerably less magical. Thank you.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: You're welcome. Magic makes an excellent demo and an awkward incident report.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And Agentis? If it coordinates the agents, why have another layer?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Coordination and product proof are different jobs. An orchestrator can assign the work; Literate A I structures the product lifecycle. This film proves the local harness, not a deployed Agentis integration.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: All right. Reluctantly, I'm convinced. It's not asking me to learn engineering again. It's asking me and my very fast colleagues to stop skipping it.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: I'll accept reluctantly. What worries you now?

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Tomorrow the framework changes. Next week my project changes. Six months later nobody remembers which copied instructions are stale. How does this stay useful?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Start with litai update as a read-only plan. It compares recorded inheritance, current local files and upstream authority. Review the classifications before applying anything.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: So it isn't git pull followed by a cheerful overwrite of my decisions.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: No. Safe upstream-only changes and local conflicts are different cases. Apply deliberately; review conflicting choices explicitly. This demonstrated revision doesn't promise automatic merging of arbitrary competing edits.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And an updated framework executable is another authority change, not the same as refreshing inherited documents.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Right. Standard-bound projects use the documented reviewed rebind after an intentional wheel upgrade. Then rebuild and verify current evidence. Old receipts don't become fresh because the version number did.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Can I put our team's conventions in one repository and let several projects inherit them? Please say the answer doesn't involve synchronized copy and paste.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: That's repository lineage. The framework can feed a team parent, which feeds applications. Components, Flavors and skills compose through recorded parent revisions; projects can add their own intent.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And our team can choose different presenters for its tutorial. I wasn't planning to become an inherited dependency.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: The video craft is reusable. We are this repository's story. Pin and review parent changes; use explicit reparenting when changing parent authority, rather than quietly pointing somewhere else.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: What about a product made of several independent repositories? That's a dependency graph, not necessarily an inheritance family.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Precisely. Orchestration keeps declared child repositories, exact pins and dependency order explicit. Review the plan, acknowledge execution, and keep each child's evidence. Inheritance and orchestration solve different problems.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: So we keep the good old tools, add a visible process, and let the fast agents do the repetitive work without appointing them sole judges of success.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: That's the adventure. Start with one useful boundary and one machine. Review the intent, run the work, inspect the evidence, then expand.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: I'm renaming final, final, really final dot zip. Apparently we can identify a release with something stronger than increasingly urgent adjectives.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: The public repository has the source, commands and limitations for this film. Tell us where you got stuck, what remained unclear, and what your real project needs.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: I'm still skeptical. But now I have a repeatable way to be skeptical. That's an upgrade I can ship.
